questions.q: When does the psalmist cry out to Yahweh, the God of his salvation?
questions.a: The psalmist cries out continually to ask Yahweh to help him.

questions.q: What does the psalmist ask Yahweh to do for him?
questions.a: He asks Yahweh to pay attention to his prayer as he cries out to him.
He is experiencing so many bad things that he feels he is about to die.

questions.q: What does the psalmist say others expect to happen to him?
questions.a: People expect him to die soon because he has so little strength left.

questions.q: What does the psalmist say about the dead who lie in the grave?
questions.a: He says that it seems as if Yahweh is no longer aware of people who have died and has stopped taking care of them.

questions.q: How does the psalmist describe where he feels as if Yahweh has placed him?
questions.a: He says it is as though Yahweh has thrown him to the bottom of a deep, dark pit.

questions.q: What feels like an oppressive burden to the psalmist?
questions.a: He feels that Yahweh is so angry with him that it feels as if he is drowning in Yahweh’s anger.

questions.q: Why do the psalmist’s acquaintances avoid him?
questions.a: Yahweh has made his illness so unpleasant that his friends stay away from him and he is not able to visit any of them.

questions.q: What does the psalmist say about his eyes?
questions.a: His eyes are swollen from crying out in prayer to Yahweh about his affliction.

questions.q: What questions does the psalmist ask Yahweh about the dead?
questions.a: He asks Yahweh if he will do a miracle to help him before he dies and is no longer able to praise Yahweh.

questions.q: What does the psalmist remind Yahweh about dead people?
questions.a: He reminds Yahweh that if he dies, he will no longer be able to talk about how kind and faithful Yahweh is or all the amazing things he does or how good he is.

questions.q: When does the psalmist’s prayer come before Yahweh?
questions.a: His prayer comes before Yahweh in the morning as if it were already there waiting for Yahweh when he gets up.

questions.q: What does the psalmist feel like Yahweh has done to him?
questions.a: The psalmist feels like Yahweh has rejected him and is ignoring him.

questions.q: How long has the psalmist been sick and on the verge of death?
questions.a: Since he was young, the psalmist has been so ill that he has nearly died.

questions.q: What does the psalmist say Yahweh’s anger has done to him?
questions.a: Because of Yahweh’s anger, the terrible illness that he has permitted has destroyed the good life the psalmist could have had.

questions.q: What have the bad things Yahweh has allowed in the psalmist’s life done to him?
questions.a: They are like floodwaters that continually surround the psalmist and are about to drown him.

commentary.text: The psalmist pours out his soul to God in lamentation.
He wrestles by faith, in his prayer to God for comfort.

Verses 1–9 The first words of the psalmist are the only words of comfort and support in this psalm. Thus greatly may good men be afflicted, and such dismal thoughts may they have about their afflictions, and such dark conclusion may they make about their end, through the power of melancholy and the weakness of faith. He complained most of God's displeasure. Even the children of God's love may sometimes think themselves children of wrath and no outward trouble can be so hard upon them as that. Probably the psalmist described his own case, yet he leads to Christ. Thus are we called to look unto Jesus, wounded and bruised for our iniquities. But the wrath of God poured the greatest bitterness into his cup. This weighed him down into darkness and the deep.

Departed souls may declare God's faithfulness, justice, and lovingkindness; but deceased bodies can neither receive God's favours in comfort, nor return them in praise. The psalmist resolved to continue in prayer, and the more so, because deliverance did not come speedily. Though our prayers are not soon answered, yet we must not give over praying. The greater our troubles, the more earnest and serious we should be in prayer. Nothing grieves a child of God so much as losing sight of him; nor is there any thing he so much dreads as God's casting off his soul. If the sun be clouded, that darkens the earth; but if the sun should leave the earth, what a dungeon would it be! Even those designed for God's favours, may for a time suffer his terrors. See how deep those terrors wounded the psalmist. If friends are put far from us by providences, or death, we have reason to look upon it as affliction. Such was the calamitous state of a good man. But the pleas here used were peculiarly suited to Christ. And we are not to think that the holy Jesus suffered for us only at Gethsemane and on Calvary. His whole life was labour and sorrow; he was afflicted as never man was, from his youth up. He was prepared for that death of which he tasted through life. No man could share in the sufferings by which other men were to be redeemed. All forsook him, and fled. Oftentimes, blessed Jesus, do we forsake thee; but do not forsake us, O take not thy Holy Spirit from us.
